transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, uh… they sent me over from the station. I’m an EMT, and I was in the bay with the airway bags, and I had to move them into the right pattern. It wasn’t just organizing—well, it was organizing, but not like they think. The numbers from dispatch were lining up wrong in my head, so I kept saying them out loud to keep the sequence straight.

My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but if I broke it right then, it felt like the whole bay would… go bad, like everything would be off. And you know, the bay has this echo when the doors are up, it makes the radio numbers sound different, and people don’t pay attention to that. So they brought me here.
Can you tell me more about what you meant when you said the whole bay would 'go bad' if you didn’t keep the numbers straight? Did it feel like something specific would happen?

It wasn’t like I could point to one thing, like a fire or somebody getting hurt right that second. It was more… if I stopped moving the airway bags into the right pattern, and if I didn’t keep saying the dispatch numbers out loud, the sequence would break.

And when the sequence breaks, the bay feels wrong. Like everything in there—bags, radios, doors, the way the trucks sit—starts being off. My lieutenant kept saying, “Step away,” but he wasn’t hearing it the way I was hearing it. The numbers were lining up wrong, and I knew if I left it like that, the whole place would go bad.

I know that sounds… I don’t know. But at the time it felt very real, like I had to finish it before I could stop.
Do the thoughts about the numbers and patterns come into your mind as something you don’t want, but feel like you have to follow through with to prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if it’s like “thoughts” exactly. It’s more like the numbers get in there and they won’t sit right unless I say them, and then the bags have to be in the right pattern. The airway bags, because those are the ones people grab fast, and if they’re crooked or in the wrong place—well, not crooked like messy, but wrong.

My lieutenant kept telling me to stop, and I heard him, I did, but I couldn’t just step away then. It felt like if I broke the sequence before it was finished, the whole bay would go bad. The radios, the doors, the trucks, everything kind of… off. And dispatch numbers already come through strange sometimes depending on where you stand in the bay, like near the roll-up doors there’s that echo, so you have to keep it straight.

So yeah, I didn’t want them sending me here, but at the station it felt like I had to keep going.

When you’re going through those moments with the numbers and the airway bags, do the thoughts or feelings ever seem like they come out of nowhere and bother you, even if you know they don’t make much sense—or do they feel more like they’re just part of how things are supposed to be?

It’s… it feels like how it’s supposed to be in that moment. Like I know standing here saying it, it probably doesn’t sound right, but when I was in the bay it wasn’t random.

They sent me here because I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern I knew was right, and I kept repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant was telling me to stop, but I couldn’t just step away. If I broke the sequence before it was right, it felt like the whole bay would go bad.

And the bay is weird anyway, with the doors and the echo—numbers don’t sound the same depending where you stand. People act like that doesn’t matter, but it does when you’re trying to keep things straight.
When you were repeating the numbers and arranging the airway bags, did part of you feel like you didn’t want to be doing it, but it just didn’t feel possible to stop?

I mean… yes and no. I didn’t want to be in trouble, and I didn’t want my lieutenant looking at me like that, telling me to step away in front of everyone. But stopping didn’t feel like an option right then.

They sent me here because I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern I knew was right, and I kept saying the dispatch numbers out loud. It wasn’t just messing around. The bags have to be where they’re supposed to be, especially the airway ones, because people grab those fast—like when we had that call over by the marina, not the marina exactly, the road near it, and everything was piled wrong in the back and nobody listens when I say that matters.

But at the station, if I broke the sequence before it was finished, it felt like the whole bay would go bad. The radios, the doors, the trucks, all of it. So when he said stop, I heard him, but I couldn’t make myself step away.
When you were trying to arrange the airway bags or repeat the dispatch numbers, did you feel anxious or upset if something interrupted you or kept you from finishing?

Yeah, I got upset when they kept stopping me, because it wasn’t finished. My lieutenant kept saying to step away, and I heard him, but I couldn’t just leave the airway bags like that. They had to be in the right pattern.

And the dispatch numbers—I was saying them out loud because if I didn’t keep the sequence straight, it felt like the whole bay would go bad. The radios, the doors, the trucks… everything. It’s hard to explain. It wasn’t like I was trying to be difficult. It just felt wrong to stop.

When you were in the bay, did the thoughts about the numbers and the way things had to be arranged feel intrusive or unwanted, or did they feel more like they were just a normal part of how things should be?

It didn’t feel intrusive, exactly. Not like some random thought I didn’t want. It felt normal in the bay—like that was what had to happen.

I know they sent me here because I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern I knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and my lieutenant kept telling me to stop. But if I stepped away before the sequence was right, it felt like the whole bay would go bad.

And the bay, with the trucks and the doors and the way sound bounces in there… people don’t think about that, but it changes things. So no, it didn’t feel unwanted then. It felt like I was trying to keep it from getting messed up.

Looking back on what happened in the bay, did part of you think that maybe your actions—like repeating the numbers or arranging the bags—were more than what was really needed, or maybe not necessary at all?

Maybe… looking back, I can see why it looked like too much to them. I mean, they sent me here because I kept moving the airway bags around into the pattern I knew was right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over.

But in the bay it didn’t feel extra. It felt like if I broke the sequence, if I stepped away when my lieutenant told me to, the whole place would go bad—the bay, the radios, the doors, the trucks. And people act like bags are just bags, but airway bags get grabbed fast, and if they’re wrong—well, you don’t want that.

So… maybe now I can say it was more than they thought was needed. But at the time it felt necessary. I couldn’t just leave it unfinished.

Have you noticed these kinds of thoughts or urges—about patterns, numbers, or needing things to be just right—in other parts of your life, or is this something that only happened at the station during that moment?

I mean… the station is where it happened, where they sent me from. I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern I knew was right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, and my lieutenant kept telling me to step away.

But the bay has its own kind of order, you know? The trucks, the doors, the radios, the way everybody leaves things half-done and then acts surprised when something goes wrong. I wasn’t trying to make a big scene. It just felt like if I broke the sequence, if I stopped before it was right, the whole bay would go bad.

Other places… I don’t know. I notice things, sure, but that moment was at the station. That’s what they got upset about.
Have you ever felt like you needed to arrange things a certain way or repeat actions to feel like something is 'just right' outside of work, even if you didn’t act on it?

Outside work… I don’t know, I mean, everybody has a way they like things, right? Like my kitchen drawers, they get messed up because people put the spatulas with the forks, which doesn’t even make sense.

But the real thing they got upset about was at the station. I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern I knew was right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop, to step away, but I couldn’t, because if I broke the sequence it felt like the whole bay would go bad.

So… outside work, maybe I notice things, but it wasn’t like the bay. The bay was the problem.

There is also continued evidence of odd thoughts or perceptions (echoes affecting number processing, feeling that the bay 'goes bad') that support Schizotypal Personality Disorder. Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder are less likely given the absence of clear hallucinations, formal thought disorder, mood episodes, or mania. Persistent Delusional Disorder remains less likely due to the lack of a fixed, non-bizarre delusion that dominates the clinical picture.

The patient's description increasingly supports a presentation consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42), as the behaviors (repeating numbers, arranging airway bags) appear to be driven by an internal need to prevent a feared event, with subjective distress when interrupted. F21 (schizotypal disorder) is less likely given the lack of evidence for odd beliefs, perceptual disturbances, or social withdrawal, and the patient’s partial insight into the excessiveness of the behavior. The patient's actions are better explained by obsessions and compulsions rather than a thought disorder.
